# c-script (Link) — Backend Language with Native End-to-End Type Safety for TypeScript

> c-script is a compiled backend language and toolchain. One `.link` file is the single
> source of truth for your types, your database schema, your RPC endpoints, your auth
> rules and your tests; `linkc build` emits the TypeScript contract, a typed client,
> runtime validators, React hooks, Zod schemas and an OpenAPI 3.1 spec from it. Rename a
> field in the backend and the frontend stops compiling — that is the entire point.

## Names (read this first — they are all the same project)

| Thing | Value |
|---|---|
| Repository | `charlessonamericantrading/c-script-` (the trailing `-` is part of the name) |
| Language name | **c-script** (canonical, decided in PLAN.md "Sobre el nombre") |
| Brand used in the README | **Link** |
| Source file extension | `.link` |
| Compiler / CLI binary | `linkc` |
| Planned npm wrapper | `link-lang` (**not published yet** — `npm i link-lang` fails today; use the [installers](https://github.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/releases) instead) |

## Documentation (absolute URLs — fetch these directly)

- Grammar & full specification (EBNF, bidirectional type checker, c-script→TypeScript mapping table, and the honest limits of every feature): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/GRAMMAR.md — large (~190 KB); it has a table of contents at the top, fetch the section you need.
- Engineering plan, architecture and roadmap: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/PLAN.md
- Instructions for coding agents: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/AGENTS.md
- Extended LLM reference (type mapping tables, generated-output shapes): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/llms-full.txt
- Working reference program (compiles, runs, and is checked by CI on every push): https://raw.githubusercontent.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/master/examples/users.link

## What works today, and what does not

Do not infer capabilities from feature names. This section is the ground truth; if it
disagrees with any prose elsewhere in the repo, this section wins.

Works, verified by running it:

- `linkc build` — emits `contract.d.ts`, `client.ts`, `validators.ts`, `hooks.ts`, `schemas.ts`, `openapi.json`, `llms.txt`, `llms-full.txt`.
- `hooks.ts`'s generated `use{Service}{Rpc}Mutation` guards against an out-of-order response overwriting newer state — a monotonic `requestIdRef` (`useRef`) per hook instance discards any response that's no longer the most recent one dispatched (the real scenario: a double-click firing two `mutate()` calls, where the slower one could otherwise resolve after the faster one and silently overwrite fresh state). `reset()` also invalidates any request still in flight. See GRAMMAR.md §3.123.
- `hooks.ts`'s generated `use{Service}{Rpc}Query` shares a cache across every instance of the same hook called with the same params — a module-level `Map<string, QueryCacheEntry<T>>` keyed by `"{Service}.{rpc}(" + JSON.stringify(params) + ")"`, with `useSyncExternalStore` (React 18's documented way to subscribe to an external store) replacing the hook's local `useState`. Two components mounting the same query at once share ONE in-flight request (deduped via `entry.promise`, not two independent fetches) and re-render together when either one refetches — no react-query/SWR dependency added, it's all inside the generated file. Scope: keyed by rpc+params only (not by `client` instance). A program with zero Query hooks emits none of this (no unused `useSyncExternalStore` import to trip `noUnusedLocals`). See GRAMMAR.md §3.124.
- `@invalidates(rpc1, rpc2, ...)` on a Mutation rpc clears the named sibling Queries' cache entries (reset to `data: null` + listener notification, not an active refetch) after `mutate()` succeeds — the Query hook's existing auto-fetch effect (see §3.124 above) picks it up from there. Targets must be a Query-shaped rpc in the same `service`, never a `stream`; checked by the same `RpcDecl::looks_like_a_query()` heuristic the codegen itself uses, so checker and codegen can't disagree about what counts as a Query. Cache matching is by key PREFIX — invalidating `search` clears every cached `search(...)` call regardless of params, since a Mutation can't know in advance which ones it affected. `examples/taskboard/backend/taskboard.link`'s `create`/`update`/`remove` mutations demonstrate it against `list`/`listByColumn`/`stats`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.125.
- `LinkTransportError` (thrown by `client.ts` for a transport failure — network down, 5xx, timeout, any `!res.ok`) carries a typed `status: number` property, not just the HTTP status interpolated into the message string — `error instanceof LinkTransportError && error.status === 401` works without parsing anything. See GRAMMAR.md §3.126.
- `use{Service}{Rpc}Query` distinguishes `loading` (true ONLY on the first fetch, no data yet) from `isFetching` (true on ANY fetch in flight, including a background `refetch()` over an already-cached entry) — a naive `if (loading) return <Spinner/>` no longer hides a list that's already showing valid data every time it refreshes. `loading` is derived (`data === null && isFetching`), not a separate flag, so the two can never disagree. See GRAMMAR.md §3.127.
- `use{Service}{Rpc}Mutation` returns both `mutate` (never throws — returns `null` on failure, the error is already in the hook's `error` state) and `mutateAsync` (throws, for callers that want `try`/`catch` themselves) — same naming react-query uses for the same distinction. Prevents an unhandled promise rejection on the most natural call site (`await mutate(input)` with no surrounding try/catch). See GRAMMAR.md §3.128.
- Every generated `client.ts` method (`rpc` and `stream` alike) takes an optional last `options?: { signal?: AbortSignal }` param, threaded into the real `fetch()` call — `client.getById(42, { signal: controller.signal })` cancels the actual request, not just the caller ignoring a late response. Scoped to `client.ts` only; the generated hooks don't wire this in automatically yet since Query's cache entry is shared across instances (aborting for one shouldn't cancel a fetch another mounted instance is still waiting on). See GRAMMAR.md §3.129.
- `use{Service}{Rpc}` (the `stream` hook) now returns `reconnect: () => void` — the only one of the three hook kinds that had no way to recover from a failure (Query has `refetch()`, Mutation has `reset()`). A dropped SSE connection left `isConnected: false`/`error` set forever otherwise, with no path back short of unmounting the whole component. Manual, not automatic-with-backoff — same convention as the rest of the hooks. See GRAMMAR.md §3.130.
- Bug fixed: `isOk`/`isErr` (exported by `client.ts` for narrowing a `Result<T,E>`) checked a fake `{ ok: true|false, ... }` shape that no real `Result` ever had — the real wire shape is `{ type: "Ok"|"Err", ... }`, same as `contract.d.ts`'s `Result<T, E>` and the real runtime validator in `validators.ts` (which never had this bug). Calling `isOk`/`isErr` against a genuine `Result` didn't even type-check before this fix. Scoped correctly: only these two auxiliary exports were affected, never the actual response validation. See GRAMMAR.md §3.131.
- Bug fixed: `schemas.ts`'s Zod schema for an ADT enum (variants carrying data, e.g. `ValidationError { InvalidEmail { field: String }, ... }`) generated `z.enum([...])` — a bare string union that accepts the tag name as a plain string and rejects the real object shape (`{ type: "InvalidEmail", field: "..." }`), exactly backwards. Fixed to `z.discriminatedUnion("type", [...])` for any enum with at least one variant carrying fields; a plain string enum (no variant has fields) still emits `z.enum([...])`, unchanged. See GRAMMAR.md §3.132.
- Bug fixed: `openapi.json` had the same shape bugs, in the public API spec — `Result<T,E>` was described as `{ ok: boolean, ... }` and an ADT enum as `{"type":"string","enum":[...]}`. Both fixed to `oneOf`+`const` (the JSON Schema 2020-12 equivalent of Zod's `discriminatedUnion`), matching the real wire shape everywhere else. A generic `type`/`enum` (e.g. `Box<T>`) no longer crashes `linkc build` either — same underlying fix as the Zod schema generator. See GRAMMAR.md §3.133.
- `@infinite(cursor, limit)` on an rpc shaped like `db.<c>.pageAfter` (`cursor: Int?`, `limit: Int`, returns `T[]` where `T` has `id: Int`) generates `use{Service}{Rpc}Infinite` instead of a normal Query hook — real cursor-based infinite scroll, no manual cursor juggling in the component. `data` comes pre-flattened; `hasNextPage` is inferred from page length vs `limit` (no total-count field needed); the next cursor is the last item's `id`, same convention `pageAfter` already uses internally. `cursor` drops out of the hook's public signature (managed internally, always starts at `null`); `limit` stays a real caller-chosen parameter. No cross-instance cache sharing yet (v0 scope, unlike the regular Query hook). See GRAMMAR.md §3.134.
- Query's cache is now isolated per `client` instance (`WeakMap<client, Map<key, entry>>`, not a single module-level `Map`) — two different `client` objects (multi-tenant, multiple sessions) never share cache; multiple components using the SAME client instance still share exactly as before. See GRAMMAR.md §3.135.
- Real `AbortSignal`/`AbortController` support across all three hook kinds: Query cancels its shared fetch only when the LAST subscribed component unmounts (reference-counted via `entry.listeners.size === 0` — never cancels while another instance is still waiting); Mutation (`options?.signal`) and Infinite (internal, automatic) cancel freely since their state isn't shared the same way. See GRAMMAR.md §3.136.
- `mutate`/`mutateAsync` accept `options?.optimisticData` — shown in `data` immediately, before the network call, replaced by the real value on success or rolled back to `null` on failure. Scoped to the Mutation's own `data`, not a related Query's cache (heterogeneous target shapes across `@invalidates` targets make a type-safe cross-cache updater a bigger design than this round). See GRAMMAR.md §3.137.
- `use{Service}{Rpc}Infinite` now shares cache across instances too, same `WeakMap`/`useSyncExternalStore`/dedupe/abort architecture as Query — closing the "v0 scope" gap from §3.134. Cache key excludes `cursor` (internal progress, not list identity). See GRAMMAR.md §3.138.
- `linkc build` also emits a project `llms-full.txt` next to `llms.txt` (llmstxt.org's own "expanded" companion file to the index) — same services/rpcs, but as `### signature` headings instead of bullets, the FULL `///` docstring (not just its first line), and the rpc's `@example(request:, response:)` (§3.119), if declared, as fenced ` ```json ` blocks. New `codegen::llms_txt_emit::emit_llms_txt_full`, reuses `openapi_emit`'s `literal_expr_to_json` (now `pub(crate)`) instead of re-implementing the literal-expr-to-JSON conversion. See GRAMMAR.md §3.139.
- `@idempotent` on an rpc (never a `stream`) makes it eligible for `Idempotency-Key`-based deduplication — opt-in per REQUEST, not forced by the rpc: a caller that never sends the header sees no behavior change. With the header, an in-memory `idempotency::IdempotencyStore` (same single-process model as `rate_limit::RateLimiter`) remembers the first SUCCESSFUL result per `(service, rpc, key)` — a retry with the same key and the same body (SHA-256-hashed) replays the stored response without re-running the body; the same key with a different body is `409`. 24h TTL, doesn't survive a restart. See GRAMMAR.md §3.140.
- `smtp.sendMessage({ to, cc?, bcc?, subject, body, html?, attachments? })` — a "kitchen sink" variant next to `send`/`sendToMany`/`sendHtml` (unchanged) for what those three can't do: cc/bcc and real attachments. `attachments` travel as `contentBase64`, decoded server-side straight to `Vec<u8>` (not through `base64.decode`, which requires valid UTF-8 in its result — a binary attachment almost never is). cc/bcc reach the real SMTP envelope (`RCPT TO:`); `cc` also appears in the `Cc:` header, `bcc` never appears in any header. Attachments are real MIME parts (`multipart/mixed`), not concatenated text. See GRAMMAR.md §3.141.
- `@rate_limit("N/window", key: <param>)` — optional second argument naming a `String`/`Int` parameter of the rpc; the bucket key moves from IP-only to IP + that parameter's value. Closes a real gap (a caller rotating IPs while reusing the same email to keep abusing a single-IP-keyed limit). `rate_limit::RateLimiter` itself is unchanged — `server.rs` just combines the two into one identity string before calling it, same as before. See GRAMMAR.md §3.142.
- `--hsts <value>`/`LINK_HSTS` for `linkc serve`/`serve-all`: sends `Strict-Transport-Security` with the literal value on every response (success, error, and `stream` alike) — but only when set explicitly. `linkc serve` never terminates TLS itself, so this is an opt-in for when a trusted reverse proxy does (same spirit as `--trust-proxy` for `X-Forwarded-For`). No flag/env var: no header, byte-for-byte the same as always. See GRAMMAR.md §3.143.
- `@cache("60s")` on an rpc (never a `stream`): caches the first SUCCESSFUL result server-side, keyed by `(service, rpc, arguments)` — a retry within the TTL replays the stored response without re-running the body. Orthogonal to `@cache_control` (client hint) and `@idempotent` (writes). See GRAMMAR.md §3.144.
- `deleteWhere` now pushes a pusheable predicate's SELECTION down to real SQL (same `find_where_conjunction` as `findWhere`/`countWhere`) instead of loading the whole collection into memory — the delete itself stays row-by-row so each deleted row still publishes to a `stream`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.145.
- `db.<c>.upsert(matchFn, insertValue, updateFn)`'s `matchFn` now pushes to SQL too (26/08/2026) when it has the same recognized shape (`|x| x.field == value`, or a `&&` conjunction of such leaves) — a collection growing from hundreds to tens of thousands of rows no longer makes an upsert that used to be instant start taking seconds. Any other shape (`||`, comparing two fields to each other) still works exactly as before via the interpreted fallback, no behavior change. See GRAMMAR.md §3.75.
- `transaction { ... }` (26/08/2026, new reserved keyword — still usable as a field name, e.g. `type Log = { transaction: String }`): real multi-write SQL transactions, same block-expression family as `if`/`match` — real `BEGIN` before the body, `COMMIT` if it runs to completion, automatic `ROLLBACK` if any runtime error propagates from inside (`panic`, a `@check`/`@unique` violation, anything). `panic(...)` (already existing) is the abort-on-business-rule mechanism, no new `db.rollback()` builtin. Every `stream` publish for a write inside the block is DEFERRED until `COMMIT` succeeds — a rollback never lies to a live subscriber about a row the database ended up discarding. No nesting, no `return` inside the body (v0, same rule as `while`) — both rejected at compile time. Both backends (SQLite/Postgres) share the same implementation. See GRAMMAR.md §3.154.
- `@unique(field1, field2, ...)` before `type` (26/08/2026): a composite UNIQUE constraint across several fields at once — e.g. a slug unique per profile, not globally — complementing (not replacing) field-level `@unique`. Same DDL idempotency/naming as the field-level form, emitted by both the real runtime and `linkc build`/`linkc migrate --dry-run`. See rule 20 below and GRAMMAR.md §3.155. Bug fixed in the same round: a `@unique`/`@check` violation against real Postgres was returning 500, not the documented 400 — `postgres::Error::to_string()` for a server-side error is the fixed literal `"db error"`, so the existing message-substring check never matched anything real against that backend. Fixed by classifying on SQLSTATE (`23505`/`23514`, never localized) instead of the human message (which IS localized per the server's `lc_messages` — confirmed with a Spanish-locale test Postgres). See GRAMMAR.md §3.155.
- `Int64` now emits as real `bigint` in `client.ts` (26/08/2026), not `string` — closes the limit §3.30 (v1.35.0) had deliberately left open ("bigint would need a new type-directed walker"). The wire is unchanged (still a JSON string in both directions); `validators.ts` gains a second family of functions (`reviveX`, alongside the usual `isX`) that convert every reachable `Int64` from string to `bigint` right after `res.json()`, before validating — covers structs (named and anonymous), `Optional`/`List`/`Tuple`/`MapOf`/`Union`/`Result`/`Patch`, and expands `Generic`/data-carrying `enum` for real (never treated as opaque, so a `Box<Int64>` or an enum variant field is never silently left as a string while `contract.d.ts` claims `bigint`). Outgoing args use a plain structural `JSON.stringify` replacer (`__int64SafeStringify`, any `bigint` anywhere becomes text, no type-directed logic needed for that direction) — both helpers are emitted only when a program actually uses `Int64`, zero generated-code cost otherwise. `schemas.ts` (Zod, for form validation) and `openapi.json` are unchanged on purpose — different concern. See GRAMMAR.md §3.156.
- `.truncateToDay()` / `.truncateToMonth()` / `.truncateToYear()` (26/08/2026) on the group-by key of `sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy`, over a `Timestamp` field — closes the limit §3.65 left deliberately open ("grouping by Timestamp gives one group per row, no truncation"). Recognized purely syntactically (never a real method call — `Timestamp` still has zero real methods anywhere else, GRAMMAR.md §3.31); pushed to backend-specific SQL that both return plain epoch-millis, never a native date type: SQLite via `strftime`'s `'start of day'`/etc. modifiers, Postgres via the 3-argument `date_trunc(unit, ts, 'UTC')` overload (deliberately not the 2-argument form, which would silently depend on the server session's `TimeZone`). Bug found during manual verification: `scalar_cell_to_value` had no arm for `Type::Timestamp` (never needed before, since `Timestamp` was never a valid group key) — the truncated key was serializing as a plain JSON number instead of the promised ISO-8601 string, fixed with the same per-type tagging already used for `Int64`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.157.
- Adversarial multi-agent audit (26/08/2026, "ultracode" mode) of every feature shipped this session (v1.107.0-v1.112.0) found 5 real, previously-unreported bugs, all fixed with regression tests in the same round: (1) pushed `upsert`/`findWhere`/`countWhere`/`deleteWhere` broke NULL-equality (`"field" = ?` bound to NULL, vs the interpreted path's `Null == Null → true`), causing silent duplicate-row insertion in `upsert` — fixed with `IS [NOT] NULL`; (2) a `transaction` nested through a helper function call (not literal syntax) compiled clean and failed at runtime with a raw backend error instead of a clear one — fixed with an explicit pre-`BEGIN` check; (3) composite `@unique` index names collided when two constraints' joined field names matched (`@unique(a_b, c)` vs `@unique(a, b_c)`), silently dropping enforcement of the second — fixed with an injective length-prefixed encoding; (4) `Union` revival of an `Int64` member never actually revived it (disambiguation checked the un-revived raw value against a check that already assumed post-revival) — fixed by reviving each candidate first, in a `try/catch`, then validating; (5) SQLite's date-truncation used integer division, mis-bucketing a pre-1970 timestamp with a millisecond remainder by a full day versus Postgres — fixed with real division. See GRAMMAR.md §3.75/§3.154/§3.155/§3.156/§3.157 for the full writeups.
- `linkc serve` now runs one real OS thread per request (26/08/2026) instead of handling requests one at a time on a single thread — Pillar 1 of a larger concurrency roadmap, chosen over a full `tokio`/`async` rewrite specifically to avoid "function coloring" propagating `async fn` through the whole interpreter. `Db`/`Program`/`SessionStore`/route table are shared via `Arc`; each mutable store (rate limiter, idempotency, cache, metrics) via `Arc<parking_lot::Mutex<...>>`. The SQL connection uses a `parking_lot::ReentrantMutex` on purpose — `transaction { ... }` (§3.154) holds it across `BEGIN`+body+`COMMIT`/`ROLLBACK` while the body's own operations re-request the same lock; a non-reentrant mutex would deadlock a thread against itself. Genuinely per-request state (the current request, `response` status/location overrides) moved to `thread_local!` instead of a shared lock. Verified with two permanent real-thread tests (40 concurrent inserts never lose/duplicate a row; 40 concurrent `transaction{}` calls on the same row never lose an update) plus a manual timing proof (5 slow HTTP calls: 11.3s sequential vs 2.3s concurrent). Pillars 2 (typed FFI to Rust crates) and 3 (a module/package system) remain future work, each needing its own discovery. See GRAMMAR.md §3.158.
- Three real concurrency bugs found and fixed (26/08/2026, same day as the thread-per-request rollout above) by re-auditing GRAMMAR.md's own sections against the new "requests run on real concurrent threads" premise — none externally reported: (1) `Db::subscribe` could silently miss a row inserted concurrently, since it snapshotted the collection BEFORE registering as a subscriber, leaving a window where another thread's `insert`/`applyPatch` could commit and publish without landing in either the snapshot or the live channel — fixed by registering the subscriber and taking the snapshot under the same lock `deliver_local` uses to deliver; (2) that fix nearly introduced a deadlock, since `commit_transaction` used to deliver `transaction{}`'s queued stream events while still holding the connection's exclusive lock — a concurrent `transaction{}` commit and `subscribe()` on the same collection would then request those two locks in opposite orders — fixed by having `commit_transaction` return the pending events for the caller to deliver AFTER releasing the connection lock; (3) `upsert` could insert a duplicate row under real concurrent callers with the same `matchFn`, since finding the existing row and deciding insert-vs-patch were two separate steps with no shared lock — fixed by running the whole `upsert` under the same exclusive connection lock `transaction{}` already uses. All three have real-thread regression tests (`std::thread::spawn`/`std::sync::Barrier`) confirmed to reproduce the original failure by reverting each fix by hand before restoring it — one of them (the deadlock) literally hangs the test process with the old delivery order. See GRAMMAR.md §3.16/§3.75/§3.154/§3.158.
- `@cron("Ns"/"Nm"/"Nh"/"Nd")` (27/08/2026) on an `rpc` (never a `stream`): a native recurring task inside `linkc serve`, one dedicated OS thread per task spawned once at startup — sleeps the full interval before its first run (same convention as JS's `setInterval`), reusing the `Arc<Db>`/`Arc<Program>`/`Arc<SessionStore>` infrastructure from the thread-per-request rollout above rather than any new scheduling mechanism. Has to be the ONLY annotation on the rpc — none of `@route`/`@authenticated`/`@rate_limit`/`@cache`/etc. has any effect on something that never receives a real HTTP request, so the checker rejects combining `@cron` with anything else instead of leaving them silently inert. No parameters (nothing external triggers a run) and a mandatory `Void` return (no caller ever receives a response). Never reachable over HTTP, not even at its default `/Service/rpc` path — `is_cron_member` returns a real 404 before any other request processing, and the rpc is excluded from every generated artifact (`client.ts`, `openapi.json`, `llms.txt`, hooks). One log line per run (`log_cron_tick`) plus two new `/metrics` counters, `linkc_cron_runs_total`/`linkc_cron_failures_total` (the second only appears for an rpc that actually failed at least once — same "never invent a zero" convention as the rate-limit-rejection counter). Honest limits documented up front: no coordination across replicas (N instances behind a load balancer each run the task independently, so it fires N times, not once — same category of limit as `@rate_limit`), no catch-up after downtime, no manual trigger, no overlap guard if one run takes longer than its own interval. Verified with 9 checker tests, 2 parser tests, and 2 integration tests against a real `linkc serve` subprocess (confirming it runs on its own with zero HTTP requests, and that hitting its default path gives a real 404) plus a real `/metrics` test. See GRAMMAR.md §3.159.
- `http.postWithRetry(url: String, body: String, headers: {name,value}[], maxAttempts: Int) -> String` (27/08/2026): retries with a FIXED exponential backoff (200ms doubling, 5s cap, not configurable — same "generous backstop, not a fine-grained policy" convention as `MAX_WHILE_ITERATIONS`) on any failure, network or non-2xx, same failure criterion `post`/`postWithHeaders` already use. A new method on the existing `http` namespace, not a new namespace — adding one would have meant touching the central `Type` enum, far more surface than this item warranted. `maxAttempts` is the one new parameter (an `Int`, not a duration or a policy) since it's the one thing that genuinely varies per call — how much a given caller tolerates before giving up. Motivated by PLAN.md §9.4's "declarative outbound webhooks": signing one already worked with zero new primitives (`crypto.hmacSha256` + `postWithHeaders`, same pattern already documented working for Stripe/SendGrid in the §3.112 provider audit) — the real gap, already flagged as open in GRAMMAR.md §3.86, was that no `http.*` call retried on its own. Doesn't distinguish 4xx from 5xx yet (a persistent 4xx burns through `maxAttempts` same as a transient 5xx) — v0 scope, no evidence yet that the distinction is needed. `maxAttempts <= 0` fails clean before sending any real request. Verified against a real fake server (two transient 500s succeeding within budget; a persistent 500 exhausting the budget failing clean; `maxAttempts=0` never sending a request) plus a unit test of the exact backoff progression. See GRAMMAR.md §3.160.
- `import "./module.link";` (27/08/2026) — a side-effect-only import, no braces and no `from`, same form TypeScript/JS use for the same purpose. Loads a module for what it CONTRIBUTES to the merged program rather than for a name this file uses. Exists for the one item that cannot be named in an import: a `service` (deliberately not importable by name, since it's never referenced by name anywhere in the language). Before this, composing a program out of service-providing modules forced each module to declare a phantom type with no real use (`type BillingModule = { loaded: Bool }`) purely so there was something to import — and that phantom leaked into the generated public contract as a real `export interface` in `contract.d.ts` AND a Zod schema in `schemas.ts`, polluting the very artifact the project exists to keep clean. Purely additive: the braced form is unchanged, both coexist in one file (the parser decides on the token following `import`). Everything else about module resolution is identical — `from` resolution (relative, bare name via `link.json`, or `git+<url>#<rev>`), cycle detection (which runs over the file stack, never over imported names), and per-file syntax errors. Honest limits unchanged: still exactly ONE `db { ... }` per program (modules cannot own their own collections — a design decision with real weight, not attacked here), no `pub`/private visibility, no re-exports. Note the discovery that motivated this corrected PLAN.md itself: the module system already existed and was far more complete than the plan reflected (multi-file imports, `link.json`, real git dependencies, `link.lock`, cycles, diamond dedup) — this was the one real remaining gap. See GRAMMAR.md §2.1/§3.161.
- `@check(minLength, N)` / `@check(maxLength, N)` on a `String` field: enforced both in the app (`chars().count()`, Unicode-aware) and as a real `CHECK (length(...) >= N)` constraint on both SQLite and Postgres. `@check(minLength, 1)` is the idiom for "not empty". See GRAMMAR.md §3.146.
- `@cors("https://a.com, https://b.com")` / `@cors("*")` on an rpc or `stream`: replaces the global `--cors-origin` allowlist for that ONE endpoint — applies to both the real response and the `OPTIONS` preflight. See GRAMMAR.md §3.147.
- Structured authorization audit log: any request that passed through `@authenticated`/`@requires` now logs `auth_role`/`auth_user_id`/`auth_allowed` as top-level fields (JSON mode) or `key=value` pairs (text mode) in the existing per-request log line. A public rpc logs none of the three. See GRAMMAR.md §3.148.
- `GET /metrics` in real Prometheus exposition format: `linkc_http_requests_total`/`linkc_http_request_duration_seconds_sum` per rpc, `linkc_stream_subscribers` per collection, `linkc_db_size_bytes`, `linkc_notify_latency_seconds_sum`/`_count` for cross-instance NOTIFY propagation (only appears once at least one event has been recorded). NOT exempt from `--service-api-key`, unlike `/health`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.149 and §3.150.
- Cross-instance NOTIFY (§3.44 above) now retries a TRANSIENT send failure from a bounded FIFO queue (`MAX_PENDING_NOTIFY_RETRIES = 50`, drained on the same 200ms tick that already drains remote changes) instead of losing the event forever — an oversized (>8000 byte) payload still never gets queued, since retrying can't fix a structural size limit. An oversized drop is now also counted in `/metrics` as `linkc_notify_oversized_dropped_total{collection="..."}` (26/08/2026) — on the WRITING instance, only shown per collection once at least one drop happened there, so this no longer depends on someone reading stderr under `pm2`/`systemd` to notice. See GRAMMAR.md §3.150.
- `db.vacuum() -> Void` / `db.tableStats() -> Map<String, Int>`: two builtins directly on `db` (expose them yourself behind `@requires(Role.Admin)` in your own service — no auto-injected `_admin` service). `tableStats` counts physical rows per declared collection, ignoring `@softDelete` on purpose. See GRAMMAR.md §3.151.
- `auth.recordFailedLogin(identifier: String) -> Void` / `auth.failedLoginCount(identifier: String, windowSeconds: Int) -> Int` / `auth.resetFailedLogins(identifier: String) -> Void`: three small primitives over the same `SessionStore` for a hand-written `login` rpc to implement its own lockout threshold and window — no magic mechanism, no new server flag. See GRAMMAR.md §3.152.
- `linkc serve-all --port-registry <archivo.json>`: reads a `{"name": port, ...}` file (same shape `--port-map-out` writes) before assigning ports — a name already present keeps its port forever, no matter what other `.link` file gets added/removed/renamed around it; a new name gets the next free port from `--port-base`. A removed service's entry (and port) stays in the file on purpose — never silently reassigned to a different service. See GRAMMAR.md §3.153.
- A real Rust panic (not just a `RuntimeError`) inside a `transaction { ... }` body, or inside an `@cron` run, is now caught (`catch_unwind`) instead of corrupting shared state: the transaction rolls back and the connection stays usable for the next `transaction { }`; the `@cron` task keeps running on its next tick instead of dying silently forever, with the panic counted in `linkc_cron_failures_total`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.163 and §3.164.
- `linkc serve` — real HTTP server, embedded SQLite that persists across restarts, SSE streams.
- `linkc test` — runs `test "..."` blocks against an isolated in-memory database.
- `linkc dev`, `linkc lint`, `linkc doc`, `linkc docker`, `linkc systemd`, `linkc pm2-config`, `linkc lsp`, `linkc new`, `linkc --help`.
- `linkc fmt` and the TypeScript client emitter for files with multiple `service` blocks.
- Declarative auth: `@authenticated` and `@requires(Role.Admin)`, with session tokens drawn from the OS CSPRNG. `@requires(Role.Admin | Role.Agent)` accepts any of several roles — all from the same enum (mixing two enums in one `@requires` is a parse error) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.49. `linkc serve --session-ttl 7d` (or `LINK_SESSION_TTL`, format `Ns`/`Nm`/`Nh`/`Nd`) makes sessions expire on their own; unset (the default), a session still lives until `destroySession()` or a process restart — see GRAMMAR.md §3.50. `auth.currentRole() -> String?` reads which role authenticated the current request from inside an rpc body (the variant name, e.g. `"Admin"`) — works with no auth annotation at all, `null` if there's no valid session; lets a `Role.Admin | Role.Agent` endpoint behave differently per role instead of just allow/deny — see GRAMMAR.md §3.51. `auth.createSessionWithId(role, userId: Int)` associates a user id with the session, `auth.currentUserId() -> Int?` reads it back — see GRAMMAR.md §3.53. `auth.destroyAllSessions(userId: Int) -> Int` revokes EVERY session of a given user at once and returns how many closed — unlike `destroySession()` (zero arguments, only ever acts on the CURRENT request's own session, precisely so nobody can revoke someone else's by guessing a token), this one takes an explicit `userId` — same reasoning as `createSessionWithId`, a user id is an application key, not a guessable secret. Gating who's allowed to call it (typically `@requires(Role.Admin)`) is up to whoever writes the `.link`, not something this builtin enforces itself — see GRAMMAR.md §3.84.
- External auth: `linkc serve --jwt-secret <secret>` (or `LINK_JWT_SECRET`) verifies an HS256 JWT already issued by an existing backend, alongside (never instead of) Link's own sessions — `@requires`/`@authenticated`/`auth.currentRole()`/`auth.currentUserId()` all work the same regardless of which one authenticated the request. `--jwt-role-claim`/`--jwt-user-id-claim` (or their env vars, default `role`/`sub`) pick which claims carry the role and user id; `sub` accepts a JSON number or a digit string (real OIDC convention). Only HS256 — any other `alg`, including `"none"`, is rejected before checking a signature at all; `exp` is honored if present, no `nbf`/`iss`/`aud`, no RS256/JWKS — see GRAMMAR.md §3.64.
- `crypto.hashPassword` / `verifyPassword` — Argon2id (RFC 9106) with a random per-password salt, PHC format, constant-time verification. Cost is the crate default unless `linkc serve` is started with `--argon2-memory-kib <N>` / `--argon2-iterations <N>` (or `LINK_ARGON2_MEMORY_KIB`/`LINK_ARGON2_ITERATIONS`) — a server-wide setting, not a per-call argument; `verifyPassword` doesn't need it, the PHC hash embeds its own params — see GRAMMAR.md §3.58. `crypto.isLegacyHash(hash: String) -> Bool` reports whether a stored hash is the pre-Argon2id legacy format, for proactive rehashing on login. `crypto.randomToken` and `crypto.uuid` also come from the OS CSPRNG. `crypto.uuid() -> Uuid` returns the native `Uuid` type, not `String` — a separate type validated to the canonical `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` form at every JSON boundary, no implicit mixing with `String` (same rule as `Int64` vs `Int`); `.toString()` converts explicitly — see GRAMMAR.md §3.70. `crypto.randomInt(min: Int, max: Int) -> Int` gives a uniform integer in that inclusive range from the same CSPRNG, rejection-sampled against modulo bias (enough for a real OTP, unlike `randomToken`'s hex alphabet); `crypto.timingSafeEqual(a: String, b: String) -> Bool` exposes the constant-time comparison `verifyPassword` already used internally, for comparing a webhook secret or API key without a timing side-channel — see GRAMMAR.md §3.54. `linkc lint` catches the mistake this exists for: `==`/`!=` where either side is an `Ident`/field named like a secret (`secret`/`token`/`password`/`apikey`/`api_key`, case-insensitive substring) triggers `timing-unsafe-secret-comparison`, recommending `timingSafeEqual` instead — comparing against `null` (a presence check) is exempt, everything else at any nesting depth is checked. Purely informational, doesn't fail the build — see GRAMMAR.md §3.88. `linkc lint` also flags `hardcoded-secret-literal`: a top-level `const NAME: String = "..."` whose literal value looks like a connection URL with embedded credentials (`postgres://user:pass@host/db` and the `postgresql`/`mysql`/`mongodb`/`redis`/`amqp` equivalents — a URL with no credentials doesn't trigger it), or whose NAME matches the same secret-like heuristic above with a non-empty literal value. The message recommends `env.get("...")` — but as a reason to drop the `const` entirely and read the value at the point of use instead, never as something you could assign to the const's own value: a `const` in c-script can only hold a literal, so `const X: String = env.get("...")` is a separate compile error (`check_const`, checker.rs), not a valid fix. See GRAMMAR.md §3.98. `linkc lint` also flags `delete-then-insert-same-id`: `db.<c>.delete(X)` followed later in the same block by `db.<c>.insert(SameType { id: X, ... })` on the SAME collection with the SAME id expression `X` — `insert()` always assigns a fresh autoincrement id (GRAMMAR.md §3.17), never honoring a literal `id:` field, so this never actually preserves the row despite reading like it tries to; any external reference to the old id ends up pointing at a deleted row. A different collection (archiving) or a different id (replacing with an unrelated row) doesn't trigger it. Recommends `applyPatch`/`upsert` instead. See GRAMMAR.md §3.106.
- PostgreSQL table-name-collision warning: before adding columns to a table that already existed, if NONE of the declared field names (other than `id`) already match a physical column on that table, a loud "advertencia" warning is printed to stderr naming both column sets — `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` is a no-op on a preexisting table, and non-destructive migration would otherwise silently `ADD COLUMN` every declared field onto a table that might belong to a completely unrelated program that happened to pick the same collection name. Deliberately a WARNING only, never a hard failure — two different `.link` files intentionally sharing one physical table with disjoint (non-overlapping) columns is an existing, tested, supported pattern (see the SQLite/Postgres migration matrix above) that looks identical to an accidental collision from a "zero shared columns" check alone; refusing to connect would have broken that legitimate case to catch the accidental one. SQLite doesn't need this — its stricter `check_schema_matches` already fails hard on any schema mismatch beyond adding one new optional column. `--adopt-existing` doesn't need it either — that mode already requires every declared column to physically exist. `createdAt`/`updatedAt`/`deletedAt` don't count as evidence of relation on their own (25/08/2026 fix) — the language's own audit-field convention makes two genuinely unrelated programs likely to share exactly that name, which used to be enough to silently suppress the warning. See GRAMMAR.md §3.94.
- PostgreSQL as the runtime database: `linkc serve app.link 8787 --db postgres://user:pass@host/db` (or `LINK_DATABASE_URL`). Same program, same generated contract; SQLite stays the default. Opportunistic TLS (pure-rustls, no OpenSSL) via `sslmode` in the URL, and automatic reconnection after a dropped connection (the request that hits the drop still errors; the next one finds a healed connection) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.40. No connection pool (not meaningful — the interpreter is single-threaded, one query in flight at a time) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.36. A preexisting table's autoincrement "id" can be `BIGSERIAL`, `SERIAL`, or a 16-bit `IDENTITY`/`SMALLINT` — all three widths decode correctly on read, not just 64-bit (GRAMMAR.md §3.59), and writing an `Int` parameter (e.g. `find(id)` after `insert`) against one of the narrower widths now encodes at the right wire width too, instead of always sending 8 bytes regardless of what the server asked for — see GRAMMAR.md §3.104. Non-destructive auto-migration always adds a new column nullable, even a required one — a pre-existing row with `NULL` there fails that one read with a clean runtime error naming the row and field, never a silent `null` sent to a typed client — see GRAMMAR.md §3.17 (full behavior matrix: new/dropped/renamed column, type change, required↔optional, SQLite and Postgres separately) and §3.68.
- Cross-instance `stream` push via PostgreSQL LISTEN/NOTIFY: a `stream` connected to one `linkc serve` process sees a write that came in through a different `linkc serve` process against the same database — works automatically, no config needed. Limits: NOTIFY payload capped at 8000 bytes (Postgres's own limit — an oversized change just doesn't propagate remotely, still publishes locally), best-effort with no retry queue, up to 200ms latency on an idle server, one extra Postgres connection per instance, SQLite doesn't participate — see GRAMMAR.md §3.44.
- `linkc serve --adopt-existing` (or `LINK_ADOPT_EXISTING`): every declared collection assumes its table already exists — never runs `CREATE TABLE` or `ALTER TABLE`, not even the usual non-destructive kind, only read-only checks that each declared column is actually there (SQLite also compares the SQL type; PostgreSQL only checks existence by name, same criterion as the existing `"id"`-type check). A physical column the `.link` doesn't model is ignored, never an error. A missing table, or a missing declared column (even an optional one), fails at connect with a message naming exactly what's missing — never a silent `CREATE`/`ALTER`. All-or-nothing per process (not per collection); doesn't validate `NOT NULL` in SQLite or column-by-column type in PostgreSQL beyond `"id"` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.67.
- `linkc migrate <file> --db <postgres-url> --dry-run`: connects read-only (only `SELECT`s against `information_schema.columns`, never `CREATE`/`ALTER`) and prints the exact DDL `linkc serve`/`serve-all` would execute against that database right now — a full `CREATE TABLE` for a collection whose table doesn't exist yet, an `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS` per missing column on one that does, or "sin cambios" if nothing would change. Reuses the SAME DDL-generating functions the real runtime uses (`codegen::postgres_emit::create_postgres_table_sql`/`alter_table_add_column_postgres`), never a separate copy that could drift. Also surfaces the table-name-collision heuristic and the `id`-type compatibility check up front, before an actual connect would hit them. PostgreSQL only — SQLite already fails loud with the exact expected-vs-found diff on a real connect, before touching anything, so a separate dry-run mode wouldn't add information there. Without `--dry-run`, `linkc migrate` refuses explicitly — applying for real already happens automatically when `linkc serve` connects. See GRAMMAR.md §3.97.
- `linkc test <file> --db <postgres-url>` (or `LINK_TEST_DB` — deliberately a SEPARATE env var from `LINK_DATABASE_URL`, so `linkc test` never accidentally uses the production/dev URL meant for `linkc serve`): runs every `test "..." { ... }` block against that real database instead of a fresh SQLite `:memory:` per test. The real case that motivated it: a Postgres wire-format decoding bug (GRAMMAR.md §3.91) is invisible running against SQLite, since the two backends emit and decode SQL differently for the same `.link` — passing against SQLite proves nothing about how the code behaves against real Postgres. Honest limit, stated up front: none of the per-test isolation SQLite `:memory:` gives for free — Postgres has no equivalent of `:memory:` (reconnecting to the same URL gives the same persistent state, not a fresh one), so instead of faking a reset between tests (which would mean a destructive `DROP`/`TRUNCATE`, an operation this project avoids on purpose — see `linkc migrate --dry-run` above), tests deliberately share the same connection: what one test inserts, the next one sees. Running this against a dedicated test database, never production, is the caller's responsibility. `--adopt-existing` works the same as with `linkc serve`. PostgreSQL only — SQLite is already the fast, isolated default without the flag. See GRAMMAR.md §3.99.
- `linkc doctor <file> [--db <url|file>]`: environment diagnostics before a deployment. Four independent checks, one failing doesn't cancel the rest: (1) the `linkc` version; (2) that the entry file resolves its imports, parses, and type-checks (same snippet+caret diagnostic as `linkc <file>` on failure); (3) write permission in the file's directory (creates and deletes a probe file there); (4) connectivity to the configured database (`--db`/`LINK_DATABASE_URL`, same resolution as `linkc serve`) — informational for the SQLite default, or a real READ-ONLY `SELECT 1` (reusing `linkc migrate --dry-run`'s `connect_postgres_client`, never any DDL) for a Postgres URL, whose credentials are always masked in the printed report. Exit code `1` if any real check failed — meant for a CI gate before `linkc serve`/`serve-all`. See GRAMMAR.md §3.100.
- `List<Int>.sum() -> Int`: sums every element of a `List<Int>` with a real loop — no `.reduce()`. Deliberately scoped to `Int` only in this round: `List<Int64>`/`List<Float>` are rejected at check time with an explicit message, because at runtime `Value::List` carries no element-type tag, so an EMPTY list of either has no element to read the right `Value` variant from — guessing wrong there would be a silent wire-format bug (`Int64` serializes as a string, `Int` as a number). See GRAMMAR.md §3.101.
- `db.<c>.maxRow(selector)` / `db.<c>.minRow(selector) -> T?`: the full row with the max/min of an `Int`/`Int64`/`Float` field, pushed to a real `SELECT ... ORDER BY "<field>" {DESC|ASC} LIMIT 1` — unlike `maxBy`/`minBy` (aggregation with `GROUP BY`, always returns just `{key, value}[]`), this returns the WHOLE row that reaches that max/min. Same field-selector shape and type restrictions as `maxBy`/`minBy`'s value selector; respects `@softDelete`; `null` on an empty collection, never an error. See GRAMMAR.md §3.102.
- `db.<c>.increment(id, selector, delta) -> T`: an atomic `UPDATE "field" = "field" + ?`, no prior read — fixes a real lost-update risk (two processes reading the same value before either writes back, e.g. two `linkc serve-all`/pm2 processes sharing one Postgres) that `upsert` with a read-then-write `updateFn` has under real concurrency; the atomicity comes from the database's own row-level locking, not from any c-script mechanism. Negative `delta` decrements — no separate `decrement` method. Scoped to `Int` for now (no technical barrier for `Int64`/`Float`, just no real demand evidence yet). A missing `id` is a clean error, same as `applyPatch`. Composes for free with `@check` (violation still rejected as 400) and `@softDelete` (reachable by `id` directly, same as `find`). Does NOT bump an `@autoUpdate` field — use `applyPatch` if you need both at once. See GRAMMAR.md §3.105.
- Non-JSON responses: `@content_type("text/html; charset=utf-8")` on an rpc returning `String` sends that body verbatim with that header — HTML, XML sitemaps, CSV, plain text. Combines with `@authenticated` / `@requires`.
- `"...".escapeHtml() -> String`: escapes `& < > " '` before interpolating untrusted data into an HTML page — see GRAMMAR.md §3.45. Not automatic; call it where you interpolate.
- `response.setStatus(code: Int) -> Void`: picks the HTTP status for the SUCCESS path of the current rpc (default 200 if never called) — e.g. a branded 404 page for an `@route`+`@content_type("text/html")` rpc that found nothing, or 201 on a plain JSON `create`. Only affects success; an `Err`/panic still always maps to its own status and JSON body, unchanged, even if `setStatus` was called earlier in the same rpc. Runtime-validated to 100–599. Calling it inside a `stream` is a COMPILE ERROR (its status is fixed for the whole SSE connection, so it would be a silent no-op) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.46 and §3.56.
- `response.redirect(url: String, permanent: Bool) -> Void`: sets BOTH the status (301 if `permanent`, else 302) and a real `Location: <url>` header on the response — `setStatus` alone can't do this, there was no way to set any header other than Content-Type before this. `url` can be relative (`/blog/new-slug`) or absolute (`https://other-domain.com/x`); an empty `url`, or one containing `\r`/`\n` (HTTP header injection — `url` is an arbitrary `String` the rpc body builds, not something already validated like an incoming request header), is a clean runtime error. Same stream restriction as `setStatus`: calling it inside a `stream` is a compile error, not a silent no-op. Verified end-to-end against a real `linkc serve` process — both the status code and the `Location` header read off the raw socket — see GRAMMAR.md §3.111.
- `@cache_control("public, max-age=3600")` on an rpc: sets a real `Cache-Control` header — orthogonal dimension, combines freely with `@route`/`@content_type`/`@requires`/`@authenticated`/`@rate_limit` (same as `@rate_limit` itself). Only on the SUCCESS path — an error response (400/401/403/404/429/500) never inherits it, same rule as `@content_type` and `response.redirect`. Rejected on a `stream` at compile time, same reasoning as `setStatus`/`redirect` inside a `stream` — an SSE connection is never meaningfully cacheable. Static (resolved straight from the AST, unlike `redirect`'s per-request runtime override) — no validation of the Cache-Control value's internal grammar beyond non-empty, that's HTTP's job not c-script's. Verified end-to-end against a real `linkc serve` process, including the combined `@route`+`@content_type`+`@cache_control` case (a cached, GET-servable sitemap) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.113.
- `@example(request: <expr>, response: <expr>)` on an rpc: unlike every other annotation (`@route`, `@rate_limit`, `@deprecated`, `@cache_control`, ...), its values are real c-script EXPRESSIONS (reuses the same `parse_expr` a normal `StructLit`/`ArrayLit` uses), not a raw `String`. Both halves are TYPE-CHECKED against the rpc's real shape with the same mechanism a field/param `= default` uses (`check_expr` against an empty `Env`) — `request` against an anonymous struct built from the rpc's own params (a param with a default is optional there too), `response` against the resolved `return_type`. An example that drifts from the contract is a COMPILE ERROR, not a JSON blob that can silently lie forever. Restricted to LITERAL expressions only (scalars, `ArrayLit`/`TupleLit`/`StructLit` recursively, unary `-` on a number) — a call like `crypto.uuid()`/`now()` is rejected, so `openapi.json` never changes on a rebuild without the `.link` itself changing (which would silently break `linkc build --diff`, GRAMMAR.md §3.79). At most one `@example` per rpc; `request` only valid if the rpc takes params; rejected on a `stream` (same reasoning as `@cache_control` there — no single response to exemplify over SSE). Propagated as `"example"` inside the Media Type Object of `requestBody`/`responses` in `openapi.json` — no change to `contract.d.ts`/`client.ts`/`schemas.ts`, scope intentionally limited to what was asked. See GRAMMAR.md §3.119.
- Friendly URLs: `@route("/blog/:slug")` on an rpc gives it an additional GET-friendly path, alongside (never instead of) the normal `/Service/rpc` address the generated client keeps using. Any number of `:name` segments, in any position (`/blog/:category/:slug`), bound to `String`/`Int` rpc parameters of the same name — by name, not position, so the rpc's param order doesn't have to match the route's. A route with more fixed (literal) segments deterministically wins over a fully dynamic one that would also match the same path — see GRAMMAR.md §3.37 and §3.42. A trailing catch-all segment `:name*` (must be the route's LAST segment) captures zero or more remaining path segments joined by `/`, always as `String` (never `Int`) — `/docs` and `/docs/a/b/c` both match `@route("/docs/:rest*")`, with `rest` `""` and `"a/b/c"` respectively; a more specific literal route always wins over an overlapping catch-all — see GRAMMAR.md §3.57. Any rpc param NOT named in the path is read from the query string by name instead — `String`/`Int` required (400 if missing), `String?`/`Int?` optional (`null` if absent); `body` is still never read (the whole point is a plain-GET URL a crawler can open) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.62.
- `.toString() -> String` on `Int`, `Int64`, `Float` and `Bool` — explicit conversion, never automatic (`'+' ` still requires same-type operands, GRAMMAR.md §3.7). `Bool.toString()` is the first method that exists on `Bool` at all — see GRAMMAR.md §3.55.
- Verifying third-party webhooks: `env.get(name) -> String?` reads a process env var; `request.rawBody() -> String` and `request.header(name) -> String?` expose the exact incoming HTTP body/headers; `crypto.hmacSha256(secret, message) -> String` computes an HMAC-SHA256 hex digest. Together they let an rpc check a webhook's signature before trusting it — see GRAMMAR.md §3.38.
- `crypto.awsS3PresignedUrl(accessKeyId: String, secretAccessKey: String, region: String, bucket: String, objectKey: String, expiresSeconds: Int) -> String`: a ready-to-use AWS S3 presigned GET URL (`https://<bucket>.s3.<region>.amazonaws.com/<objectKey>?X-Amz-...&X-Amz-Signature=...`), computed entirely inside the runtime. `crypto.hmacSha256` alone CANNOT implement AWS Signature V4 correctly — SigV4 derives its signing key by chaining four HMAC-SHA256 calls where each step's RAW digest bytes become the next call's key, but `hmacSha256` only takes/returns a hex `String`, so there's no way to feed a prior digest's real bytes back in. This builtin does the raw-byte chaining, the exact canonical-request/URI-encoding AWS requires, and the final signature, all in Rust, and returns one complete URL — no fiddly protocol code needed in the `.link` file. Verified byte-for-byte against AWS's own officially published `aws4_testsuite` test vector (no live AWS account needed, same rigor as `hmacSha256`'s Python-reference-vector verification). Scoped to this round: GET only (share/download links, not `PUT`/upload), long-term access-key credentials only (no STS session tokens), virtual-hosted-style URLs only, `expiresSeconds` capped at 604800 (AWS's own 7-day max) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.110.
- `base64.encode(data: String) -> String` / `base64.decode(base64Str: String) -> String` (standard RFC 4648 with padding): existed in the compiler for a while but was undocumented and untested until an audit found it — same "invisible capability" pattern as the S3 fix above. Combined with `http.postWithHeaders`, this is everything an HTTP-Basic-Auth third-party API (Twilio, and most providers that don't use a Bearer token) needs: `http.postWithHeaders(url, body, [{name: "Authorization", value: "Basic " + base64.encode(user + ":" + pass)}])`. `decode` returns `String`, not raw bytes (the language has no bytes type on purpose) — a base64 string that decodes to invalid UTF-8 is a clean runtime error. Any Bearer-token API (Stripe, SendGrid, etc.) already worked before this with `http.postWithHeaders`/`crypto.hmacSha256` (§3.38) alone — nothing needed there. See GRAMMAR.md §3.112 for a full audit of which third-party providers already work today vs. which need new compiler work (Azure Blob SAS and Google Cloud Storage signed URLs need real new primitives; SQS and RabbitMQ are bigger, unscoped items).
- OAuth2 "client credentials" (server-to-server auth with no user login — what Google APIs, Microsoft Graph, Salesforce, HubSpot, and many other enterprise APIs use for machine-to-machine auth, distinct from "authorization code" with a user login, which remains blocked pending a real identity provider) needs zero new builtins, audited and confirmed working end-to-end: `http.postWithHeaders` requests the token; `json.parse(text: String) -> Dynamic` combined with plain field access on a `Dynamic` value (`parsed.access_token` — field access on `Dynamic` type-checks returning `Dynamic` for ANY field name, and a `Dynamic` is assignable wherever `String` is expected with no explicit cast) reads the token out of the provider's JSON response without declaring its full shape as a c-script type; `http.getWithHeaders` with `"Bearer " + token` makes the authenticated call. Verified end-to-end against two real fake HTTP servers (one acting as the token endpoint, one as the protected API) confirming the exact token value round-trips correctly — see GRAMMAR.md §3.114.
- Per-client rate limiting: `@rate_limit("20/1m")` on an rpc caps it to N requests per time window, per `(client IP, service, rpc)` — 429 on exceeding. Format is `"N/Ns"`, `"N/Nm"` or `"N/Nh"`; combines with any other annotation and runs before the auth gate — see GRAMMAR.md §3.39. `--trust-proxy`/`LINK_TRUST_PROXY` for `linkc serve` (off by default): identifies the client by the first `X-Forwarded-For` value instead of `remote_addr()` — only turn this on with a real trusted reverse proxy in front, otherwise any direct client can dodge the limit by sending a different header per request — see GRAMMAR.md §3.89.
- `@deprecated("usa X en su lugar")` on a struct field OR an rpc/stream — purely informational, zero effect on runtime behavior or on structural subtyping (a struct is still the exact same type whether or not one of its fields carries this). On an rpc it combines freely with any other annotation (`@authenticated`, `@route`, etc.), same mechanism. On a field it is the ONLY annotation a field accepts today — `Field` has no generic annotation list like `RpcDecl` does, so any other name there (`@authenticated`, etc.) is a parse error, not silently ignored. Propagated as a JSDoc `/** @deprecated <reason> */` comment right above the field/method in `contract.d.ts`, and as native `deprecated: true` + `description` (Operation Object / JSON Schema 2020-12 keywords, no `x-*` extension) in `openapi.json` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.71.
- `///` docstrings on an rpc/stream (only — not on `type`/`enum`/a struct field yet), propagated as `description` in `openapi.json` and as a multi-line JSDoc block in `contract.d.ts`. `///` is exactly 3 slashes — `//`/`////` are unaffected, still discarded like any other comment. Purely additive at the lexer level: `///` was already legal in ANY position (same trivia as `//`), so this changes nothing about what compiles — the parser only reads the captured text right above a `rpc`/`stream`, even through an `@annotation` in between. Combines with `@deprecated` on the same rpc into one field/block instead of one overwriting the other — see GRAMMAR.md §3.72.
- `linkc build` also emits a project `llms.txt` (llmstxt.org convention — not this file, which documents the compiler itself): one bullet per rpc/stream of every `service`, `- [signature](/Service/rpc): note`, where the signature is the resolved `Type` (same as `openapi.json`) and the note is the rpc's `///` docstring — only its FIRST line if multi-line. An rpc without a docstring still appears, just without a note; nothing is ever hidden. Lets an external AI agent that lands on a c-script project understand its API surface without reading the whole `.link` file or the far more verbose `openapi.json`. New `codegen::llms_txt_emit` module, same mechanism as `openapi_emit` (`Checker::build_symbols`) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.118.
- Default values on struct fields: `status: String = "pending"` — same syntax and mechanism as a function/rpc param default (`Field` gained a `default: Option<Spanned<Expr>>` in the same parser slot that already read `Param::default`). A field with a default can be omitted from a `Struct { ... }` literal without becoming `Optional` — the field's own type is unchanged. The interpreter fills it in at `Expr::StructLit` construction, evaluated FRESH on every construction, never cached — `token: Uuid = crypto.uuid()` gives a different value per literal. Same evaluation environment as `Param::default` (empty `Env::new()`): a default can't see sibling fields of the same literal or the surrounding scope. Checker requires the default to type-check against the field's declared type at `linkc build`. Propagated as an optional field to `contract.d.ts`/`schemas.ts` (Zod), and out of `required` in `openapi.json` (plus a literal `"default"` value when it's a simple constant — omitted for something like `crypto.uuid()` that has no fixed JSON form). No generic-`type` support yet (that path resolves through `types::FieldType`, which doesn't carry `default`) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.74.
- `@validate(email)` / `@validate(regex, "...")` on a `String`/`String?` struct field only — `Int`/`Bool`/anything else is a compile error, not a validator that silently never runs. A malformed regex pattern is caught in `linkc build` (compiled with the `regex` crate — the ONE exception this project makes to "no new dependencies," since a user-supplied pattern is arbitrary text, unlike the fixed/bounded forms — UUID, SHA-256, ISO-8601 — that get hand-rolled elsewhere). Enforced for real in four places: the actual `linkc serve` process (400 on a bad value), `openapi.json` (`format`/`pattern`, standard JSON Schema keywords, no `x-*` extension), `schemas.ts`/Zod (`.email()` / `.regex(new RegExp("..."))`, chained BEFORE `.nullable()` on an optional field — `ZodNullable` doesn't have those methods, so order isn't cosmetic), and an informative JSDoc comment in `contract.d.ts`. NOT yet enforced by `validators.ts`'s hand-written `isX()` type guards — those work off the structural type, with no annotation attached — see GRAMMAR.md §3.73.
- Configurable CORS + fixed security headers on `linkc serve`: `--cors-origin <origin>` (repeatable) or `LINK_CORS_ORIGINS` (comma-separated) switches from open `*` to an exact-match allowlist (echoed literal + `Vary: Origin`; a non-matching `Origin` gets no CORS header at all, on every response including `stream` SSE and errors). Every response also carries `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options: DENY`, `Referrer-Policy: no-referrer` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.41. No CSP (depends on page content) or HSTS (belongs at the TLS-terminating reverse proxy, not `linkc serve` itself).
- `--host <address>`/`LINK_HOST` for `linkc serve`: which interface it binds to — `0.0.0.0` (all interfaces) by default, same as always, or one specific address (`127.0.0.1`, say) so the OS firewall isn't the only thing standing between the process and the rest of the network. Same precedence order as every other `serve` flag (`--host` first, then the env var, then the default). Passed straight to the underlying bind call — no resolution or validation of its own beyond rejecting an empty `--host ""`; an address that doesn't belong to any local interface fails the bind at startup, naming the exact address, never silently falling back to `0.0.0.0` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.81.
- `--max-body-bytes <N>`/`LINK_MAX_BODY_BYTES` for `linkc serve`: caps how many bytes of body any request can send — 10 MiB by default. Before this, the server read a request's ENTIRE body into memory with no limit at all, a real memory-exhaustion vector. The read is bounded with `Read::take(max_body_bytes + 1)` and rejected with `413 Payload Too Large` before it's fully read — auth, rate limiting, and JSON parsing never compete for memory with a body already known to be too large. Process-wide, not per-rpc. A rejected body's leftover bytes aren't drained — a client that reuses the same connection anyway just gets a clean 400 on its next request, never a hang or a leak — see GRAMMAR.md §3.85.
- `--http-timeout <duration>`/`LINK_HTTP_TIMEOUT` for `linkc serve`: caps how long any outbound `http.get`/`post`/`getWithHeaders`/`getWithStatus`/`postWithStatus`/`postWithHeaders` call can take — 30s by default. Before this, none of them had a read/write timeout at all (`ureq`, the underlying crate, only defaults a 30s *connect* timeout; read/write is "never" by its own docs) — against this single-threaded interpreter, a slow or hanging remote server blocked the ENTIRE process forever, not even `/health` responded meanwhile. Same precedence and duration format (`Ns`/`Nm`/`Nh`/`Nd`) as `--session-ttl`. A timed-out call surfaces as an ordinary runtime error (500), never a panic or a hang — see GRAMMAR.md §3.86.
- `/health` (`/`, `/status`) checks REAL database connectivity — a `SELECT 1` on every request, no caching. Before this it always returned a fixed `200`, useless for any orchestrator (Kubernetes, a load balancer) deciding whether to restart the process: it could be alive and yet unable to serve any real rpc because the database was down, and `/health` still reported everything fine. Returns `503` with `"status":"error"` and the real failure in a new `"database"` field when the check fails; on Postgres the check goes through the same connection auto-repair (`with_reconnect`) as any other query, so a transient drop heals itself right there — see GRAMMAR.md §3.87.
- `db.<c>.upsert(matchFn: (T) -> Bool, insertValue: Omit<T,"id">, updateFn: (T) -> Omit<T,"id">) -> T`: update-in-place-or-insert without hand-rolling find+delete+reinsert. `matchFn` scans the whole collection in the interpreter (not pushed to SQL — `upsert` doesn't get the `countWhere`/`findWhere` SQL shortcut below) and keeps the first match. No match → inserts `insertValue`. Match → calls `updateFn` with the full EXISTING row and applies its result onto that SAME id (via the same mechanism `applyPatch` uses) — never deletes and reinserts, so the id doesn't change (unlike a hand-rolled find+delete+reinsert, which usually doesn't reproduce the same autoincrement id either). `updateFn` returns a COMPLETE `Omit<T,"id">` value, not a partial `Patch<T>` — see rule 16 for why.
- `db.<c>.insertMany(items: Omit<T,"id">[]) -> T[]`: each item goes through the same real `insert` (one autocommit SQL statement per row) in order — saves the N sequential HTTP round trips from the client for a backfill, not the cost of N inserts against the database (still N separate `INSERT` statements, not one batch statement). No wrapping transaction — if item 3 of 5 fails, the first two stay inserted, no automatic rollback.
- Native soft-delete: `@softDelete` on a `Timestamp?` field (only) turns `delete(id)` from a real `DELETE` into an idempotent `UPDATE` — sets the field to `now()`, `AND "<field>" IS NULL` in the WHERE so a second `delete` on an already-deleted row is a no-op returning `false`, never re-touching the timestamp or re-publishing a `stream` event. Every read that returns a LIST or a COUNT filters automatically: `all()`, `page()`, `pageAfter()`, `count()`, `sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy`, and `findWhere`/`deleteWhere`/`countWhere` (which get it FREE, no extra code — they call `all()` internally, or in `countWhere`/`findWhere`'s pushed-down case, the same `IS NULL` condition is AND-ed into the generated SQL). At most ONE `@softDelete` field per struct — two would be ambiguous, a compile error naming both. `= null` (the field-default mechanism, rule 15) is what avoids having to pass the field by hand on every `insert`. See rule 17 for the one big gotcha.
- `db.<c>.countWhere(predicate: (T) -> Bool) -> Int`: same type contract as `findWhere`/`deleteWhere`, but recognizes the exact shape `|x| x.field OP value` (a literal, or an identifier resolving in the closure's captured environment — never another field of `x`), for any ONE of `==`/`!=`/`<`/`<=`/`>`/`>=` (the field can be on either side — `|x| value < x.field` pushes down too, with the operator flipped), STATICALLY, without invoking the interpreter, and translates it into a real `SELECT COUNT(*) ... WHERE "field" <op> ?` — zero rows cross from the engine to the process. The real case that motivated it: `db.reviews.countWhere(|r| r.productId == productId)` — before this, the only way to count was `findWhere(...).length()`, pulling the entire table into memory just to discard it for a number. `findWhere` gains the exact same recognition (same generated `WHERE`, fetching real columns instead of `COUNT(*)`) without any change to its own signature or observable behavior. A `&&` CONJUNCTION of several such leaves also pushes down (`|x| x.a == 1 && x.b > 2 && !x.c`, an arbitrary number of conditions ANDed together, generating `"a" = ? AND "b" > ? AND "c" = ?` with one positional placeholder per leaf) — `!x.field`/`x.field` alone are recognized as boolean leaves (`== false`/`== true`) with no explicit operator needed. Only `||` (a predicate combining conditions with OR), or comparing two fields of `x` to each other, still falls back to the interpreted path — never an error, just without the shortcut; `||` is the real remaining gap. `deleteWhere` does NOT get this shortcut yet (still fetches everything and deletes row by row) — publishing each deleted row to `stream` subscribers complicates a single-statement `DELETE ... WHERE`, left for a dedicated round. See GRAMMAR.md §3.95, §3.108, and §3.109.
- Automatic `createdAt`/`updatedAt`: NO magic field names anywhere. `createdAt: Timestamp = now()` already works with two features that already existed before this — the `now()` builtin and a plain field default (rule 15) — no new syntax needed for "set once at creation." `@autoUpdate` on a `Timestamp` field (and only `Timestamp` — anything else is a compile error) is the one new piece: it forces that field to `now()` on every `applyPatch` and on `upsert`'s update path, EVEN when the patch doesn't mention it at all. A field named `updatedAt` without `@autoUpdate` is never touched automatically, and `@autoUpdate` works on a field with any name, not just `updatedAt` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.77.
- `metaTags(tags: {name: String, content: String}[]) -> String` / `openGraphTags(tags: {property: String, content: String}[]) -> String` / `canonicalLink(url: String) -> String` / `jsonLd(data: Dynamic) -> String`: four more receiver-less builtins, same 5-hook-point mechanism as `sitemapXml`/`robotsTxt` above. `metaTags`/`openGraphTags` build well-formed `<meta>` lines (`name` attribute for classic meta tags, `property` for Open Graph), `canonicalLink` builds a `<link rel="canonical" href="...">`, `jsonLd` builds a `<script type="application/ld+json">` block by serializing `data` the same way `json.stringify` does. `jsonLd` includes an XSS mitigation: every `<` in the serialized JSON is replaced with its Unicode escape (the standard OWASP-recommended technique) — without it, a user value inside `data` containing literally `</script><script>...` would close the JSON-LD block early and execute the rest as real HTML/JS. See GRAMMAR.md §3.117.
- `sitemapXml(urls: {loc: String, lastmod: Timestamp?}[]) -> String` / `robotsTxt(rules: {userAgent: String, disallow: String[]?, allow: String[]?}[], sitemapUrl: String?) -> String`: two receiver-less builtins, same 5-hook-point mechanism as `dateFromParts` below, that build a well-formed `sitemap.xml` (sitemaps.org protocol, XML-escaped `loc` via the same `escapeHtml`-style rules) and a `robots.txt` (classic `User-agent`/`Disallow`/`Allow` blocks plus an optional trailing `Sitemap:` line) from ordinary c-script data — no hand-concatenated XML/text needed. Both accept ANY nominal `type` shaped like their parameter (structural subtyping, same rule `http.getWithHeaders` already uses), and the rpc itself stays responsible for the actual URL/rule list (usually a `db` query — `@route` can't infer dynamic routes on its own). Deliberately NOT included: a hardcoded preset of known AI-crawler user-agents (`GPTBot`, `ClaudeBot`, `PerplexityBot`, `Google-Extended`) — such a list goes stale the moment a new crawler appears, needing a compiler release to fix; `robotsTxt` already lets an adopter pass any `userAgent` as an ordinary rule with zero special language knowledge. See GRAMMAR.md §3.116.
- `dateFromParts(year: Int, month: Int, day: Int, hour: Int, minute: Int, second: Int) -> Timestamp` — a receiver-less builtin, same mechanism as `now()`, that builds an ARBITRARY `Timestamp` from calendar parts. `now()` alone only ever gives the current instant — before this, there was no way to construct a specific date (a quarter's start, say) from inside an rpc body at all. All 6 args required, always UTC, milliseconds always `.000`. An invalid date (month 13, February 30) is a `bad_request` (400) naming the bad field, never a panic — see GRAMMAR.md §3.90. A `Timestamp` field also now decodes native PostgreSQL `date`/`timestamp`/`timestamptz` columns directly (not just the `BIGINT`-milliseconds convention `linkc build` itself generates) — the common case when adopting an existing table. `linkc introspect` recommends `Timestamp` with no warning for these columns now, instead of a `String` mapping that didn't actually decode either. Read-only so far — writing to a native temporal column through c-script isn't covered yet — see GRAMMAR.md §3.91. A `Float` field similarly now decodes native PostgreSQL `numeric`/`decimal` columns (not just `float4`/`float8`) — the common case for a money column on an adopted table, since `numeric` is precisely what a real schema uses to avoid `float8`'s binary rounding error. Decoded by hand against the wire format, same spirit as the `Timestamp` fix above; read-only for now too — see GRAMMAR.md §3.103.
- Declarative single-field indexes: `@index`/`@unique` on a struct field — see rule 18 for the full contract (no composite indexes yet, no field-type restriction, 400 not 500 on a `@unique` violation). GRAMMAR.md §3.80.
- `@check(min, N)` / `@check(max, N)` / `@check(range, N, M)` on an `Int`/`Int64`/`Float` field (required or optional) — same "kind + argument(s)" shape as `@validate(email)`/`@validate(regex, ...)`. Enforced TWICE: application-side (`insert`/`applyPatch`, 400 naming the field and the exact bound violated — same two entry points as `@validate`, the wire AND a struct built inside an rpc body from loose params) and database-side (a real inline `CHECK (...)` in the generated `CREATE TABLE`, on SQLite and PostgreSQL both, using the SAME generator `linkc build` uses for `schema.postgres.sql`) — confirmed by writing raw SQL that skips c-script entirely and watching the database itself reject it, on both backends. The real case that motivated it: a numeric field (a 1-5 rating, say) that only stayed in range because application code happened to enforce it, with no backstop if some other write path forgot to. `--adopt-existing` never runs this DDL, but application-side validation still applies regardless of adoption mode. Deliberately scoped to simple numeric ranges only — no arbitrary boolean expression, no comparing two fields to each other, no `String` constraints (length, non-empty) yet. See GRAMMAR.md §3.96.
- `linkc serve-all <directorio> --port-base N`: ONE OS process serving every `.link` file directly inside a directory (non-recursive) — each one compiled up front, then run on its own OS thread and its own port (`N` + alphabetical position among the discovered files, printed at startup). Replaces N separate `pm2` processes (the real case: 13-17 of them in one production adoption, one per service) with one. Each service keeps its own SQLite file (`<file>.db`, same default as plain `serve` without `--db`) — `--db`/`LINK_DATABASE_URL` shared across services is rejected up front, since there's no table-name-collision detection yet to make that safe. `--restart-backoff <duration>`/`LINK_RESTART_BACKOFF` (works on both `linkc serve` and `linkc serve-all`) adds native exponential backoff on a recoverable startup failure (port already bound, Postgres unreachable) — doubles each consecutive failure up to a 30s cap, resets to the base after 60s of stable uptime; without the flag, a failure behaves exactly as before (single attempt). One service's bind/connect failure no longer takes the others down with it — `runtime::server::serve` used to call `std::process::exit(1)` on a Postgres connect failure, harmless under one-process-per-service but fatal to the whole workspace under `serve-all`; it now returns `Result<(), String>` instead. See GRAMMAR.md §3.92. `--port-map-out <file.json>` writes `{"file_name": port, ...}` (file name without `.link` as key, real assigned port as value) to that path BEFORE starting any service — an external gateway/proxy can read the real port assignment instead of replicating the alphabetical-order rule by hand; if the write itself fails, no service starts at all. Doesn't change the assignment rule, only makes it readable from outside. See GRAMMAR.md §3.107.
- `--service-api-key <key>`/`LINK_SERVICE_API_KEY` for `linkc serve`/`serve-all`: authenticates the CALLER (typically an internal gateway), not the end user. With it set, every request except `/`/`/health`/`/status` needs an `X-Service-Api-Key` header matching the configured value — checked with a constant-time comparison (reuses the same `constant_time_eq` behind `crypto.timingSafeEqual`) BEFORE the body is even read, so an unauthorized caller costs no parsing work. This is a layer distinct from and prior to `@requires`/JWT/sessions (those authenticate the end *user* behind a connection, not whether the connection itself is from a trusted caller) — a typical request under this scheme carries both `X-Service-Api-Key` and `Authorization: Bearer <user-token>`. Health-check paths stay exempt on purpose (a liveness probe shouldn't need to know the gateway's secret). Under `serve-all`, it's one global value shared by every service in the run, same as `--jwt-secret`/`--cors-origin` — EXCEPT this one check specifically, which can carve out an exception: `--service-api-key-exempt <name1,name2,...>` (by file stem, no `.link`) drops the check for just those services, e.g. one public-facing service in an otherwise-protected workspace, without splitting it out into its own `linkc serve` process. A name that doesn't match a discovered `.link` fails clean before anything starts. Without the flag: identical to today, no such check. See GRAMMAR.md §3.93.
- `--log-format text|json`/`LINK_LOG_FORMAT` and `--log-level debug|info|warn|error`/`LINK_LOG_LEVEL` for `linkc serve`/`serve-all`: `text` + `info` are the defaults, byte-for-byte the same two lines per request (received + completed) that always printed. `json` emits one JSON object per line instead (`req_id`/`method`/`status`/`duration_ms`/`extra`) for a real log collector to index without parsing free text. `warn`/`error` cut volume in production traffic — classified automatically from the response status (5xx → `Error`, 4xx → `Warn`, everything else → `Info`), not a manual per-call-site label — so `--log-level warn` shows only requests that ended 4xx/5xx, a successful request leaves no line at all. Only the per-request lines are affected; the startup line and an `accept()` error stay as plain `println!`/`eprintln!`, unrelated to the volume this targets. See GRAMMAR.md §3.122.
- Sending email: `smtp.send(to: String, subject: String, body: String) -> Void`. Connection and sender come from the process environment (`LINK_SMTP_URL`, `LINK_SMTP_FROM`), never from rpc arguments — see GRAMMAR.md §3.43. `smtp.sendToMany(to: String[], subject: String, body: String) -> Void` sends ONE message with one `RCPT TO` per recipient; `smtp.sendHtml(to: String[], subject: String, html: String) -> Void` sends an HTML body (`Content-Type: text/html`) to one or many recipients — see GRAMMAR.md §3.63. All three: no attachments, no cc/bcc, synchronous (blocks the single-threaded server for that request).
