- Calling third-party APIs: `http.get(url: String) -> String` / `http.post(url: String, body: String) -> String` (unchanged), plus `http.getWithHeaders(url: String, headers) -> String` / `http.postWithHeaders(url: String, body: String, headers) -> String` for calls that need `Authorization` or any other header. `headers` is `{name: String, value: String}[]` — structural, not a builtin type, so any struct you declare with those two fields works. Response is only the body as `String`; a non-2xx becomes a runtime error (not a value with the status code) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.47. `http.getWithStatus(url: String, headers) -> {status: Int, headers: {name:String,value:String}[], body: String}` / `http.postWithStatus(url: String, body: String, headers) -> same` — two ADDITIONAL methods (the four above are unchanged) that return the status code and response headers as data instead of turning a non-2xx into a runtime error; the return type is structural too, no builtin name — see GRAMMAR.md §3.60.
- `db.<collection>.page(limit: Int, offset: Int) -> T[]`: real pagination — `LIMIT`/`OFFSET` pushed into the actual SQL query on both SQLite and Postgres, not `all().take(n)` (which fetches the whole table first). Same `ORDER BY "id"` as `all()` so pages don't overlap or skip rows. Negative `limit`/`offset` is a runtime error (rejected before reaching SQL, since SQLite and Postgres treat a negative value differently); an `offset` past the end is an empty list, not an error — see GRAMMAR.md §3.48. `db.<collection>.pageAfter(cursor: Int?, limit: Int) -> T[]`: cursor-based alternative for sequential/infinite-scroll pagination — the cursor is the last-seen `id` (`null` for the first page); unlike `OFFSET`, `WHERE "id" > cursor` is stable under concurrent inserts (a row written between two calls never shifts the next page) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.61.

Does NOT work today — do not propose designs that depend on these:

- **Auto HTML escaping.** `"...".escapeHtml()` exists (GRAMMAR.md §3.45, escapes `& < > " '`) but is opt-in — nothing forces you to call it. Pages are still built by concatenating `String`; interpolate untrusted data through `.escapeHtml()` yourself, or it goes into the page as-is.
- **`request.rawBody()` needs a JSON body.** Argument parsing runs before any rpc regardless of its parameter count, so a non-JSON body never reaches the rpc — a JSON webhook payload with extra fields is fine.
- **`@rate_limit` is per-process, in-memory.** No persistence across restarts, no coordination across replicas — running N replicas behind a load balancer silently dilutes the real limit (each process still enforces its own quota correctly, but the aggregate across replicas can be N× what the `.link` asked for). `linkc_rate_limit_rejections_total{method="..."}` in `/metrics` (26/08/2026) doesn't fix the dilution (would need shared state across processes, e.g. Redis — out of scope without real demand) but makes real 429 rejections visible per rpc, aggregable across replicas with a normal Prometheus query. The client IP comes from the real TCP connection by default — never `X-Forwarded-For` unless `--trust-proxy`/`LINK_TRUST_PROXY` explicitly opts into it (off by default; behind a real reverse proxy, `remote_addr()` is always the proxy's own IP, sharing the limit across every real user — see GRAMMAR.md §3.89).
- **`http.get`/`http.post`/`getWithHeaders`/`postWithHeaders` only return the response body.** No status code or response headers exposed to the program — a 4xx/5xx from the called API is a generic runtime error, not something the rpc can branch on.
- **No `ctx.user` / full caller identity.** `auth.currentRole() -> String?` (GRAMMAR.md §3.51) exposes only the role name — the session never stores a reference to the actual `User` who logged in, only the role tag, same as v0.
- **Native WASM codegen** (`linkc wasm`) is deliberately frozen at integer/boolean scalar functions.
- **No npm package yet.** Prebuilt binaries are on [GitHub Releases](https://github.com/charlessonamericantrading/c-script-/releases); `npm i link-lang` is not published.

## The rules an LLM gets wrong

Every one of these was a real bug in this repository's own documentation. They are the
difference between code that compiles and code that does not.

1. **An enum variant used as a VALUE needs braces**: `Role.Member {}`, not `Role.Member`.
   Inside an annotation it is written without braces: `@requires(Role.Admin)`. Inside a
   `match` pattern, also without braces: `Filter.All => ...`. This single rule causes most
   first-attempt failures.
2. **Closures take no return-type annotation**: `|t: Todo| { !t.completed }`, never
   `|t: Todo| -> Bool { ... }`.
3. **A `T?` still can't be dereferenced via `if`.** `if x != null` type-checks as a boolean
   test but doesn't narrow `x`, so `x.field` inside the branch is still an error — that part
   is deliberate and unchanged. Real narrowing exists through `match` instead:
   `match x { v: T => v.field, null => ... }` binds `v` to the real `T` (GRAMMAR.md §3.69).
   For "give me a default," `x ?? default` is shorter; `x.isSome()`/`x.isNone()` cover "just
   need to know if there's a value" without reading it.
4. **`db.<c>.insert` takes the type without `id`** (`Omit<T, "id">`). Passing a full struct
   with an explicit `id` is accepted, but the value is ignored — the database assigns 1, 2, 3…
5. **`db.<c>.subscribe()` is legal in exactly one place**: as the entire body of
   `stream f() -> T { while true { db.<c>.subscribe() } }`. Anywhere else it is an error.
6. **`Patch<T>` has no literal syntax.** It arrives as an RPC parameter and is passed
   straight to `applyPatch(id, patch)`.
7. **Default parameter values work** (`rpc list(limit: Int = 20)`), including enums — but
   the default obeys rule 1: `rpc list(f: Filter = Filter.All {})`.

8. **`@content_type` only goes on an rpc returning `String`** — never on a `stream`
   (SSE owns its content type), and at most once. Auth annotations stack with it:
   `@requires(Role.Admin) @content_type("text/html")` is valid and is how an admin
   page is written.
9. **`@route`'s path params must be a SUBSET of the rpc's params, matched by name.**
   `@route("/blog/:category/:slug")` requires the rpc to take `category` and `slug`
   somewhere in its params (any order — binding is by name, not position), each
   `String` or `Int`. Any rpc param NOT in the path is read from the query string
   instead (`String`/`Int` required, `String?`/`Int?` optional, `null` if absent) — a
   route with no `:param` at all still works with query-only params, or zero params.
   `body` is still never read on a `@route` GET.
10. **`@rate_limit`'s argument is `"N/window"`, not a sentence.** `"20/1m"` (20 per
    minute), never `"20 per minute"` or `"20/minute"`. Window unit is exactly one of
    `s`/`m`/`h`; the window's number is optional (`"5/m"` means `"5/1m"`) but the
    unit is not.
11. **`sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy`'s selectors must be `|item: T| { item.field }`,
    a bare field access — with the closure braces (rule 2 still applies: no `-> Type`).
    `|o: Order| { o.amount + 1 }` or any other derived expression, method call, or nested
    access is rejected at compile time: it can't be pushed to SQL — the ONE exception is the
    group-by key, which also accepts `|s: Sale| { s.at.truncateToDay() }` (or
    `truncateToMonth`/`truncateToYear`) over a `Timestamp` field, the only place in the whole
    language a method exists on `Timestamp` at all (GRAMMAR.md §3.157) — never a real method
    call, purely a syntactic shape the checker/runtime recognize (same idea as
    `db.<c>.subscribe()`'s fixed shape). Group-by is otherwise restricted to
    `String`/`Int`/`Int64`/`Bool`/`enum` fields (`Float` still rejected; a bare, untruncated
    `Timestamp` still rejected too — GRAMMAR.md §3.65); the aggregated field for
    `sumBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy` must be
    `Int`/`Int64`/`Float` — an `Int64` result stays `Int64` (string on the wire, §3.30), never
    silently narrowed to `Int`. Neither selector may point at an optional field (`f?: T` or
    `f: T?`).
12. **`Uuid` is not `String` and doesn't mix with it implicitly.** `crypto.uuid()` returns
    `Uuid`, not `String` — `"id: " + crypto.uuid()` is a compile error, same rule as `Int64`
    vs `Int`. Call `.toString()` first to get a plain `String` (then any `String` method works
    on it normally). A `Uuid`-typed field/param rejects anything that isn't the canonical
    `xxxxxxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxx-xxxxxxxxxxxx` form (8-4-4-4-12 hex) — see GRAMMAR.md §3.70.
13. **A struct field accepts a FIXED set of annotations — `@deprecated("reason")`,
    `@validate(...)`, `@autoUpdate`, `@softDelete`, `@index`, `@unique` — nothing else.**
    `RpcDecl` has a general `Vec<Annotation>` (`@authenticated`/`@route`/`@rate_limit`/etc. all
    combine freely there), but `Field` does not — writing `@authenticated legacyPhone: String`
    on a struct field is a parse error, not something the checker rejects later. At most one of
    each per field (a second `@deprecated`/`@validate`/`@autoUpdate`/`@softDelete` on the same
    field is a parse error), and `@index`/`@unique` count as the SAME slot — at most one of the
    two together, also rejected in the parser (rule 18). All the different kinds combine freely
    with each other on the same field (`@unique @deprecated("...") email: String` is fine).
    `@deprecated` is purely informational: never affects type-checking, structural subtyping, or
    runtime behavior — only JSDoc + `openapi.json` metadata (GRAMMAR.md §3.71). `@validate` is
    NOT purely informational — see rule 14.
14. **`@validate(email)` / `@validate(regex, "...")` only goes on a `String`/`String?` field,
    and is REAL enforcement, not just documentation.** `Int`/`Bool`/anything else is a compile
    error. A malformed regex pattern fails `linkc build` itself (compiled with the `regex`
    crate at compile time). At runtime, `linkc serve` actually rejects a bad value with 400 —
    this is not cosmetic, checked both when an rpc receives the whole struct as a param AND
    when the rpc builds it inline from loose params inside the body (the far more common
    shape — `rpc register(email: String) -> User { db.users.insert(NewUser { email: email }) }`
    — this is the path that needed a SEPARATE fix in `Expr::StructLit`, found by curling a real
    running server, not by reading the code). Three gotchas: (a) `@validate` is tied to the
    EXACT declaration it's written on, never inherited structurally — the "New*"
    (`Omit<T,"id">`) shape used everywhere for `insert` is a separate type from the "full" one,
    so annotate both or the create path stays unprotected; (b) the regex syntax is Rust's
    `regex` crate server-side and native JS `RegExp` in `schemas.ts` — both are PCRE-like but
    NOT identical (no backreferences in either; lookaround exists in JS but not in Rust's
    `regex`), so a pattern using lookaround compiles fine into `schemas.ts` but fails
    `linkc build`; (c) `validators.ts`'s hand-written `isX(x): x is X` type guards do NOT
    enforce `@validate` yet (they work off the structural type with no annotation attached) —
    `openapi.json`, `schemas.ts`, `contract.d.ts`, and the real server all do. See GRAMMAR.md
    §3.73.
15. **A field default (`status: String = "pending"`) does NOT make the field's type `Optional`
    — it's still plain `String`, both inside and outside the literal.** It only means the
    field can be OMITTED from a `Struct { ... }` literal; the interpreter fills in the real
    value at construction. The default expression cannot see sibling fields of the same
    literal (`{ a: Int, b: Int = a + 1 }` doesn't work — same `Env::new()`-only rule as
    `Param::default` for other rpc params) and it's evaluated FRESH every construction, not
    once — `token: Uuid = crypto.uuid()` is a different value each time, never cached. Two
    gotchas: (a) same "tied to the exact declaration" rule as `@validate` (rule 14) — the
    "New*" (`Omit<T,"id">`) shape needs its own `= default` repeated, the "full" type's default
    doesn't apply to a different type just because the field name matches; (b) no support yet
    on a generic `type` (`type Box<T> = { value: T, tag: String = "x" }` — that path resolves
    through `types::FieldType`, which doesn't carry `default`). See GRAMMAR.md §3.74.
16. **`db.<c>.upsert`'s `updateFn` returns `Omit<T,"id">`, never `Patch<T>` — this is not
    optional, `Patch<T>` literally cannot be produced from inside a function body.** `Patch<T>`
    has no literal syntax anywhere in the language (rule 6) — the ONLY way a `Patch<T>`-typed
    value exists is decoded straight off the wire as an rpc parameter. So `updateFn: (T) ->
    Patch<T>` would be unimplementable: there's no expression a closure body could return that
    types as `Patch<T>`. `updateFn` gets the full EXISTING row and returns a complete new value
    (a normal `NewX { ... }`-shaped literal) instead — still lets the update depend on the old
    row's other fields (`count: c.count + 1`), just not as a sparse patch. `matchFn` isn't
    pushed to SQL (same as `findWhere`/`deleteWhere`) and keeps only the FIRST match if more
    than one row qualifies — not atomic across multiple `linkc serve` instances against the
    same database. See GRAMMAR.md §3.75.
17. **`@softDelete`: `find(id)` does NOT filter — a soft-deleted row is still reachable by
    direct id lookup.** Deliberate, not an oversight: `insert`/`applyPatch` re-fetch the row
    they just wrote through this SAME code path, and `applyPatch` can still write the
    `@softDelete` field like any other field of `Patch<T>` — if `find`-style lookup filtered,
    an `applyPatch` that happened to touch that field would make its own post-write re-fetch
    come back empty, a panic instead of a clean result. So only LIST/COUNT-returning reads
    filter (`all`/`page`/`pageAfter`/`count`/the `*By` aggregates/`findWhere`/`deleteWhere`) —
    single-row `find(id)` never does. No `includeDeleted` escape hatch on the filtered methods
    either — direct `find(id)` is the only way to see a soft-deleted row today. See GRAMMAR.md
    §3.78.
18. **`@index`/`@unique` (field-level) are single-FIELD only, and neither annotation requires a
    particular field type** (unlike `@autoUpdate`/`@softDelete`, which are restricted to
    `Timestamp`/`Timestamp?`). At most one of the two per field. For a composite (multi-field)
    UNIQUE constraint, use `@unique(field1, field2, ...)` on the `type` itself instead (26/08/2026,
    rule 20 below) — a completely separate annotation (`type`-level, at least 2 fields), not an
    extension of this field-level one. The field-level index is created for real at startup in
    BOTH backends — `CREATE [UNIQUE] INDEX IF NOT EXISTS "idx_<table>_<field>" ...`, idempotent,
    same deterministic name every restart — and `linkc build` emits the identical statement in the
    static Postgres DDL. A `@unique` violation on `insert`/`applyPatch` (and `upsert`'s update
    path) comes back as a 400 — classified by SQLSTATE against Postgres (`23505`, locale-
    independent — the earlier substring-match on the English message string was a real bug,
    fixed 26/08/2026, see rule 20) and by the literal message against SQLite (`UNIQUE constraint
    failed`, never localized there). Any other SQL failure is still a plain 500. `--adopt-existing`
    never runs this DDL, same rule as the rest of the schema in adopt mode. See GRAMMAR.md §3.80.
19. **`panic(...)` types as `Void`, not a bottom/never type — a guard clause that calls it needs
    an explicit empty `else {}`, and has to be a STATEMENT, not the tail.** `if cond { panic(...); }`
    with nothing after it (used as the block's tail) is a compile error whenever the expected
    type isn't `Void` — `panic`'s branch produces `Void`, which doesn't unify with e.g. `Order`.
    The working guard-clause shape (the one `transaction { ... }`, GRAMMAR.md §3.154, almost
    always needs): `if cond { panic("..."); } else { }` as a STATEMENT (something else follows
    it in the block, so the whole `if` is checked against `Void`, and an empty `else` block also
    types as `Void`) — never as the last thing in the block. For an EXPECTED, recoverable
    failure (as opposed to "this should never happen"), `Result<T,E>`/`Result.Err{}` is almost
    always the better fit than `panic` — see GRAMMAR.md §3.5.
20. **`@unique(field1, field2, ...)` before `type` is a composite constraint — a different
    annotation from field-level `@unique`, not the same one with a list.** `@unique(a, b)` needs
    at least 2 fields (a single one is a compile error — use field-level `@unique` for that), each
    naming a real field of the struct; the `type` has to actually be a struct (not an alias like
    `type Ids = Int[]`); and two `@unique(...)` on the same `type` can't declare the exact same
    field set (order doesn't matter — `@unique(a, b)` and `@unique(b, a)` count as the same
    declaration). Multiple `@unique(...)` with DIFFERENT field sets on the same `type` are fine,
    each gets its own index. See GRAMMAR.md §3.155.

Collection methods, in full: `all()`, `count()`, `find(id) -> T?`, `findWhere(pred) -> T[]`,
`page(limit: Int, offset: Int) -> T[]` (LIMIT/OFFSET pushed to real SQL, not `all().take(n)`
— see GRAMMAR.md §3.48), `insert(Omit<T,"id">) -> T`, `insertMany(items) -> T[]` (GRAMMAR.md
§3.76), `applyPatch(id, patch) -> T`, `delete(id) -> Bool`, `deleteWhere(pred) -> Int`,
`subscribe()` (see rule 5), `upsert(matchFn, insertValue, updateFn) -> T` (see rule 16 and
GRAMMAR.md §3.75), `sumBy`/`countBy`/`avgBy`/`maxBy`/`minBy` (`GROUP BY` pushed to real SQL —
see rule 11 and GRAMMAR.md §3.52). `delete`/`deleteWhere` become soft-delete-aware `UPDATE`s
instead of real `DELETE`s when the collection's type has an `@softDelete` field (rule 17).

## CLI

```bash
linkc new my-app --template nextjs   # or: vite, minimal
linkc build backend.link src/gen     # TypeScript contract, client, validators, OpenAPI
linkc build backend.link src/gen --diff old-contract.d.ts  # show what changed vs. a saved contract.d.ts (PR review)
linkc test backend.link              # run the test blocks
linkc test backend.link --filter usuario  # only test blocks whose name contains 'usuario'
linkc test backend.link --db postgres://... # run test blocks against real Postgres, not SQLite :memory:
linkc serve backend.link 8787        # HTTP + SQLite + SSE
linkc dev backend.link src/gen 8787  # rebuild and restart on change
linkc introspect postgres://... > main.link  # generate a starting .link from an existing PostgreSQL schema
linkc migrate backend.link --db postgres://... --dry-run  # show the exact DDL 'linkc serve' would run, without running it
linkc doctor backend.link --db postgres://...  # environment diagnostics before a deployment: version, parse/typecheck, write permission, read-only DB connectivity
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --adopt-existing  # never touch DDL; assume every table already exists
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --host 127.0.0.1  # bind loopback only, not 0.0.0.0
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --max-body-bytes 1000000  # cap request bodies at 1 MB (default 10 MiB)
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --http-timeout 10s  # cap outbound http.* calls (default 30s)
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --trust-proxy  # @rate_limit uses X-Forwarded-For (only behind a trusted proxy)
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --restart-backoff 1s  # native exponential backoff on a port-bind/DB-connect failure
linkc serve-all ./services --port-base 3000  # one process serves every .link in ./services, one thread+port each
linkc serve-all ./services --port-base 3000 --port-map-out ./services/ports.json  # write {"name": port, ...} before serving
linkc serve-all ./services --port-base 3000 --port-registry ./services/ports.json  # same shape, but read back first -- a name keeps its port forever
linkc serve backend.link 8787 --service-api-key s3cr3t  # require X-Service-Api-Key on every non-health request
linkc serve-all ./services --port-base 3000 --service-api-key s3cr3t --service-api-key-exempt webhooks  # every service but "webhooks" requires the header
linkc --version                      # linkc 1.121.0 -- same version stamped in every generated file
```

## Verified example

This program compiles and its test passes. It is re-verified on every CI run by
`compiler/tests/docs_examples.rs`, which is what the `linkc:check` marker below means —
every c-script block in this repository's documentation is compiled by the real binary,
so an example that stops working breaks the build.

<!-- linkc:check -->
```rust
type Todo = {
  id: Int,
  title: String,
  completed: Bool,
  createdAt: Timestamp,
}

// The creation shape: the same fields as Todo without `id` (Omit<Todo, "id">).
type NewTodo = {
  title: String,
  completed: Bool,
  createdAt: Timestamp,
}

enum Filter { All, Pending, Done }

db {
  todos: Todo[],
}

service Todos {
  // Note `Filter.All {}`: an enum variant in expression position needs braces.
  rpc list(filter: Filter = Filter.All {}) -> Todo[] {
    match filter {
      Filter.All => db.todos.all(),
      Filter.Pending => db.todos.findWhere(|t: Todo| { !t.completed }),
      Filter.Done => db.todos.findWhere(|t: Todo| { t.completed }),
    }
  }

  rpc create(title: String) -> Todo {
    db.todos.insert(NewTodo {
      title: title,
      completed: false,
      createdAt: now(),
    })
  }

  // Returns Todo? and hands it to TypeScript as `Todo | null` -- no need to
  // narrow it here since this rpc just passes it through. If you DID need to
  // read a field off it in the backend, `match`/`??`/`.isSome()` narrow a
  // T? for real; `if x != null { x.field }` still doesn't.
  rpc getById(id: Int) -> Todo? {
    db.todos.find(id)
  }

  rpc update(id: Int, patch: Patch<Todo>) -> Todo {
    db.todos.applyPatch(id, patch)
  }

  rpc remove(id: Int) -> Bool {
    db.todos.delete(id)
  }

  // Live push over Server-Sent Events. This exact shape is the only legal
  // position for subscribe().
  stream watch() -> Todo {
    while true {
      db.todos.subscribe()
    }
  }
}

test "a new todo gets an id and starts pending" {
  let created = Todos.create("Learn c-script");
  assert(created.id > 0, "insert assigns the id");
  assert(created.completed == false, "a new todo starts pending");
  assert(Todos.list(Filter.Pending {}).length() == 1, "it shows up under Pending");
}
```

The TypeScript side consumes it with full inference:

```ts
import { createClient } from "./gen/client";

const api = createClient("http://localhost:8787");
const todo = await api.Todos.create("Learn c-script"); // todo: Todo
for await (const t of api.Todos.watch()) console.log(t.title);
```
